newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan announces anti-debt, austerity plans.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan announces anti-debt, austerity plans.

text.p: Pakistan's new Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif announced austerity plans on Sunday to reduce foreign debts, urging overseas Pakistanis to make donations and open hard currency bank accounts at home.
In his first televised address since party's landslide victory in February 3 elections, he said he would make "a big cut" in government expenditure, except on defence.
To help low-income groups, he announced a freeze in electricity and petrol prices, raised salaries of junior government workers and called for similar increases in the private sector.
Sharif, who has yet to name his cabinet, tried to reaasure foreign investors by saying that if necessary his government would give constitutional protection to their investments.
In his "remove debts, build the country" campaign, he appealed to overseas Pakistanis to send hard currency in the shape of donations or interest-free loans to the government.
He said he would send personal letters of thanks to those who deposited $100,000 to $1 million and those depositing $1 million or more would be invited to Pakistan to receive special medals.
He announced a donation of 10 million rupees ($248,600) from his own family, which owns the large Ittefaq group of industries.
Sharif accused past rulers of looting Pakistan for their luxuries and burdening it with $30 billion dollars in debts so that "we have lost even freedom to make our own budget."

"We are unable to protect our people from inflation," he said. "What sort of independence is this that the Pakistani government does not have the power to protect its citizens from high prices (and) our creditors are giving us orders...."
Pakistani politicians have often accused the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) of dictating economic policy as a condition for providing loans.

Sharif earlier met an IMF official. The Finance Ministry said an agreement with the fund on a standby loan was still on track and a fund mission would visit Pakistan soon to review its economic performance.

The IMF resumed and expanded a standby loan in December after the caretaker government promised to cut the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
The IMF has been anxious to know whether Sharif is fully committed to the targets agreed with the fund.
He said: "The time has come to make a pledge on the ruins of the destruction of half a century that we will take back our independence. We will tie stones on our stomachs but will get rid of debts."
As a personal example of austerity, Sharif said he would not spend a penny on himself from state funds and would not use an official car unless necessary for state functions.
The central government and the provinces would have small cabinets and each minister and senior official would use only one car, he said.
He also announced a ban on smoking on public transport and a two-year ban on elaborate banquets at wedding parties, where he said only soft drinks should be served.
